{"outside":"A heavy, very tough green stone. In a live creek it is smooth: flowing water scours it \"so that a smooth skin is produced\", while out of the water \"a rough weathered skin develops\" (Leaming 1978 p.16). \"The weathering of nephrite commonly produces a pronounced weathering rind, ranging in color from whitish gray to brownish\" (Mustoe 2024 p.15), so a boulder on a slope can look like a pale, dull rock until it is chipped or wetted.","colour":"\"Although green is the usual colour of nephrite it may range from white to nearly black through various tints and shades of green\" (Leaming 1978 p.6). Washington pieces \"commonly have colors that range from light green to dark green\" (Mustoe 2024 p.14), with small black specks: \"Dark flecks are a common feature of Washington State nephrite\" (p.20). The beach \"black jade\" is dark green to black.","checks":"A knife will not scratch it: \"The hardness of nephrite is commonly stated as 6 1/2 or slightly harder than steel. This is a useful field test to eliminate many greenish rocks such as serpentine or talc\" (Leaming 1978 p.6). It will not break: it \"may resist breakage even by an 8 lb. sledge hammer\". It is heavy for its size (about three times water). A sure answer needs a lab: \"Positive identification of a nephrite specimen requires confirmation that the main component is the mineral tremolite with a nephritic texture.\"","not_it":"Serpentine: \"Serpentine is commonly used as a substitute for jade\"; it is softer, and a knife scratches it. Green garnet rock, which is what Oregon's river and beach \"jade\" mostly is: grossularite garnet \"resembles true jadeite (jade) and nephrite, in hardness, specific gravity, toughness, greasy appearance, and feel, that it is sometimes mistaken for the other two\" (Dake 1938, DOGAMI Bull. 7 p.15); it is harder and heavier. On the salt-water beaches the white \"mutton-fat jade\" is quartz rock. A piece labelled jadeite from Washington is almost never that.","care":"DUST. Nephrite is a massive form of the same minerals as amphibole asbestos. A study of jade carvers found that \"the air samples contained intact asbestiform tremolite fibres\", even with wet cutting (Yang and others 2013), and the federal health institute calls the risk from such stone \"inconclusive\", which is not the same as safe (NIOSH 2011). Cut and grind it wet, with a respirator, outdoors, and never dry. The serpentinite it sits in can hold asbestos too: do not hammer the host rock. And much of the Darrington ground is claimed: \"About 30 active claims presently exist near Mount Higgins\" (Mustoe 2024 p.7). Read the land line."}

it travels, and far. "They rarely are found in place, usually occurring in boulders of pebbles in stream gravels" (USGS Bull. 1042-G p.219). "The physical toughness of the felted texture makes nephrite resistant to abrasion, and the well-rounded morphology of many placer specimens is evidence that they have been transported by high-energy streams from the source outcrop" (Mustoe 2024, Minerals p.19). The model carries it down the streams with the wear of the most durable stones (agate's rate: a convention, no source measures it), and thins it as bigger rivers add their own gravel.
